people.name: Nellie Stone Johnson
people.field: Labor organizing, civil rights, public office
body: In 1945, Minneapolis voters did something they had never done before: they elected a Black citizen to a citywide office. The winner was Nellie Stone Johnson, a union organizer. Her new seat was on the Minneapolis Library Board. It may sound like a small post, but it was a milestone.

Johnson was born in 1905 in Dakota County, where her family farmed for a few years; they later moved to a farm in Pine County, about 14 miles east of Hinckley. She left home as a teenager, moved to Minneapolis, went to work and finished her high school education through a University of Minnesota program. She became a labor organizer, helped organize the integrated hotel workers' Local 665, and in 1936 was elected its vice president.

Some context helps here. In the mid-twentieth century, labor unions were one of the main ways workers won better wages and safer jobs. In northern states like Minnesota, Black Americans also faced job and housing discrimination even where the law did not formally require segregation. Johnson worked on both problems at once.

She was also a political builder. In 1944 she represented the Farmer-Labor Party in its merger with the Minnesota Democratic Party. The result, the Democratic-Farmer-Labor Party (DFL), still shapes Minnesota politics today. In the late 1940s she helped establish Minneapolis's first Fair Employment Commission. In the 1950s she pushed for Minnesota's fair employment and fair housing laws, passed in 1955 and 1957, which made it illegal to refuse someone a job or a home because of race.

Johnson stayed active for decades. In a 1991 interview she said she managed Van White's 1979 campaign; White became the first African American elected to the Minneapolis City Council. She died in Minneapolis on April 2, 2002, at age 96. Nellie Stone Johnson Elementary School in Minneapolis carries her name.
keyFacts: 1905: Born in Dakota County; grew up on a Pine County farm near Hinckley; later moved to Minneapolis.
1936: Elected vice president of hotel workers' Local 665.
1944: Represented the Farmer-Labor Party in the merger that created the DFL.
1945: Elected to the Minneapolis Library Board, the first Black person elected to citywide office in Minneapolis.
1955 and 1957: Minnesota's fair employment and fair housing laws, which she championed, were enacted.
1979: Managed Van White's Minneapolis City Council campaign, by her own account.
April 2, 2002: Died; a Minneapolis elementary school is named for her.

people.name: Hubert H. Humphrey
body: In July 1948, a 37-year-old mayor from Minneapolis walked to the podium at the Democratic National Convention in Philadelphia. Hubert Humphrey knew the issue could split his party. In a short, forceful speech, he urged his party to get out of the shadow of "states' rights," the argument Southern states used to defend segregation, and to stand openly for human rights. The delegates adopted a strong civil rights plank. By NPR's account, the Mississippi delegation and about half of Alabama's, about three dozen delegates, walked out.

Humphrey grew up in South Dakota, where his father ran a drugstore. He later studied at the University of Minnesota and made Minnesota his political home. He lost a race for mayor of Minneapolis in 1943, then won in a landslide in 1945. During his time as mayor, community leaders including Nellie Stone Johnson won the creation of the city's first fair employment commission.

Some context helps here. In the 1940s the Democratic Party included many Southern politicians who supported racial segregation. The 1948 speech is remembered as a turning point in moving the national party toward supporting full legal rights for Black Americans and other minorities.

Minnesota sent Humphrey to the U.S. Senate in 1948. He served as Vice President under Lyndon B. Johnson from 1965 to 1969 and ran for president in 1968, losing narrowly to Richard Nixon. He later returned to the Senate and served until his death from cancer in January 1978.
The University of Minnesota's Humphrey School of Public Affairs carries his name and trains people for careers in public service.
keyFacts: 1911: Born in Wallace, South Dakota.
1945: Elected mayor of Minneapolis after losing in 1943.
July 14, 1948: Delivered his civil rights speech at the Democratic National Convention in Philadelphia.
1948: Elected to the U.S. Senate from Minnesota.
1965–1969: Served as U.S. Vice President under Lyndon B. Johnson.
1978: Died while serving in the U.S. Senate.

people.name: Roy Wilkins
body: As a student at the University of Minnesota in the early 1920s, Roy Wilkins wrote for the campus newspaper, the Minnesota Daily. In 1921 he also joined the St. Paul branch of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP). Writing and organizing defined the rest of his life.

Wilkins was born in St. Louis, Missouri, in 1901. After his mother died, he and his siblings were raised by an aunt and uncle in St. Paul. He graduated from the University of Minnesota in 1923 and moved to Kansas City, Missouri, to edit a Black weekly newspaper, the Kansas City Call. There he saw a far harsher system of segregation than he had known in St. Paul.

The NAACP, founded in 1909, worked mainly through the courts, lawmakers and public education to end legal segregation and protect voting rights. Wilkins joined its national staff as assistant secretary in 1931 and in 1934 succeeded W. E. B. Du Bois as editor of its magazine, The Crisis. He served as acting executive secretary from 1949 and led the organization from 1955 until 1977, first as executive secretary and, from 1964, as executive director.

Those years covered the Montgomery bus boycott, the 1963 March on Washington, the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965. Wilkins favored legal and legislative methods: steady pressure on Congress and presidents.
President Lyndon B. Johnson awarded Wilkins the Presidential Medal of Freedom. He died in 1981. The Roy Wilkins Auditorium in St. Paul bears his name.
keyFacts: 1901: Born in St. Louis, Missouri; raised by relatives in St. Paul.
1921: Joined the St. Paul branch of the NAACP.
1923: Graduated from the University of Minnesota, where he wrote for the Minnesota Daily; then edited the Kansas City Call.
1955–1977: Led the NAACP (title changed to executive director in 1964).
Received the Presidential Medal of Freedom from President Johnson.
1981: Died.

people.name: Mee Moua
people.field: Public office, Asian American civil rights advocacy
body: In early 2002, a seat in the Minnesota Senate opened up on St. Paul's East Side. A 32-year-old lawyer named Mee Moua, little known in politics, decided to run. She won the special election on January 29, 2002, with about 51 percent of the vote (3,055 votes) in a four-way race. With that victory she became the first Hmong American elected to any state legislature in the United States.

Moua was born on June 30, 1969, in Xieng Khouang, Laos. The Hmong are an ethnic group from the mountains of Laos and neighboring countries. During the Vietnam War, many Hmong men fought alongside U.S. forces in what is often called the "Secret War" in Laos. Moua's family fled to a refugee camp in Thailand, where they spent several years, and came to the United States when she was nine. She grew up in Appleton, Wisconsin.

Moua graduated from Brown University in 1992, earned a master's degree in public affairs from the University of Texas LBJ School in 1995, and received her law degree from the University of Minnesota in 1997.

In the Senate, Moua represented St. Paul's District 67 from 2002 to early 2011 and was re-elected twice. From 2007 to 2010 she chaired the Senate Judiciary Committee, overseeing courts and criminal law.

After leaving the Senate, she served as a vice president at the Asian and Pacific Islander American Health Forum and then for five years as president and executive director of Asian Americans Advancing Justice | AAJC, a national civil rights organization in Washington, D.C. She left that post in March 2017. The Carnegie Corporation of New York named her one of its Great Immigrants in 2013.
keyFacts: June 30, 1969: Born in Xieng Khouang, Laos.
Childhood: Several years in a Thai refugee camp; arrived in the U.S. at age nine; grew up in Appleton, Wisconsin.
1997: Earned her law degree from the University of Minnesota.
January 29, 2002: Won a special election to the Minnesota Senate, becoming the first Hmong American elected to a U.S. state legislature.
Senate service: Re-elected twice; chaired the Senate Judiciary Committee (2007–2010); term ended January 2011.
To March 2017: Led Asian Americans Advancing Justice | AAJC in Washington, D.C.

people.name: Frances Perkins
people.field: Social welfare policy, labor, public service
body: On March 25, 1911, Frances Perkins was having tea near Washington Square Park in New York City when she heard fire engines. She ran toward the noise and watched the Triangle Shirtwaist Factory burn. The fire killed 146 workers, most of them young immigrant women. Perkins later described that day as a turning point in her life.

Perkins was born in Boston in 1880 and studied at Mount Holyoke College. She had already volunteered at Chicago settlement houses, including Hull House, community centers in poor neighborhoods that offered education and services to immigrants. After the fire, a citizens' Committee on Safety was formed, and Perkins became its executive secretary. She then served as an investigator and expert witness for New York's Factory Investigating Commission, whose work led to some of the strongest workplace safety laws in the country.

When Franklin D. Roosevelt became president in 1933, during the Great Depression, he chose Perkins as Secretary of Labor. She was the first woman to serve in a U.S. presidential cabinet, and she held the job for all twelve years of his presidency, longer than any other Secretary of Labor.

Before the 1930s the United States had almost no national safety net. Older people, the unemployed and people with disabilities depended mostly on family, charity or local relief. Perkins chaired the Committee on Economic Security, whose work led to the Social Security Act of 1935. That law created old-age pensions and unemployment insurance and laid the groundwork for aid to families with children and for later disability programs. She also helped shape laws setting a federal minimum wage and limiting child labor.

After leaving the cabinet, she served on the U.S. Civil Service Commission until 1953 and then taught at Cornell University's School of Industrial and Labor Relations. She died in New York City on May 14, 1965.
keyFacts: 1880: Born in Boston.
March 25, 1911: Witnessed the Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire, in which 146 people died.
1933–1945: U.S. Secretary of Labor, the first woman in a presidential cabinet.
1935: Chaired the committee whose work produced the Social Security Act.
May 14, 1965: Died in New York City.

people.name: Fannie Lou Hamer
body: On August 31, 1962, Fannie Lou Hamer boarded a bus with seventeen other Black residents of Sunflower County, Mississippi, and rode to the county courthouse in Indianola to try to register to vote. She was 44. That night, the owner of the plantation where she had worked as a timekeeper and sharecropper for eighteen years ordered her to leave.

Hamer was born in 1917, the youngest of twenty children in a family of sharecroppers. Sharecropping was a system common in the South after slavery ended, in which families farmed land owned by someone else in exchange for a share of the crop. It often trapped families in debt and poverty.

Losing her home did not stop her. She went to work with the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC), a youth-led civil rights group, helping other Black Mississippians register. In the early 1960s, Black citizens in Mississippi were kept from voting through unfair tests, fees, threats and violence. In June 1963, Hamer and other activists were arrested in Winona, Mississippi, and she was badly beaten in the county jail.

In 1964 she helped lead the Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party, which challenged the all-white official delegation to the Democratic National Convention in Atlantic City. On August 22, 1964, she testified before the convention's Credentials Committee, describing the eviction and the beating. President Lyndon Johnson interrupted the live coverage with an impromptu press conference, but her words reached the public anyway.

Her activism helped build pressure for the Voting Rights Act of 1965. In 1969 she bought land for the Freedom Farm Cooperative, to help poor families in Mississippi grow food and gain economic independence. She died in 1977.
keyFacts: 1917: Born in Mississippi to a sharecropping family, the youngest of 20 children.
August 31, 1962: Tried to register to vote in Indianola, Mississippi; was forced off the plantation where she had lived for eighteen years.
1963: Arrested and beaten in jail in Winona, Mississippi.
August 22, 1964: Testified before the Democratic National Convention's Credentials Committee.
1969: Bought land for the Freedom Farm Cooperative.
1977: Died.

people.name: Ed Roberts
people.field: Disability rights, independent living, public service
body: At age 14, Ed Roberts contracted polio. The illness left him paralyzed in most of his body and dependent on a respirator, and he spent long hours in an iron lung. Years later, when he sought help from California's vocational rehabilitation agency, it labeled him unemployable. In 1975, Governor Jerry Brown appointed him director of that same state rehabilitation department.

Roberts was born on January 23, 1939, in San Mateo, California. In 1962 he became the first severely disabled student to live on the University of California, Berkeley campus, housed in a ward of Cowell Hospital with his iron lung. Other students with disabilities soon joined him. Together they formed a group called the Rolling Quads, which pressed the university to make buildings and services accessible.

Some context helps here. For much of American history, people with significant disabilities were often placed in institutions or kept at home, with decisions made for them by doctors and families. Roberts and his peers argued that disabled people should control their own lives, choose their own personal care assistants and live in the community. This became known as the independent living movement.

In 1972, the first Center for Independent Living opened in Berkeley, run by and for people with disabilities. Roberts served as its executive director from 1973 to 1975. Others also played central founding roles, so he is best described as a leader of the movement rather than its sole founder.

As state rehabilitation director from 1975 to 1983, Roberts helped shift public services toward supporting people to live independently. In 1983 he co-founded the World Institute on Disability in Oakland. He received a MacArthur Fellowship in 1984. He died in Berkeley on March 14, 1995. California observes Ed Roberts Day on January 23, his birthday.
keyFacts: January 23, 1939: Born in San Mateo, California.
At 14: Contracted polio.
1962: Enrolled at the University of California, Berkeley; later helped form the Rolling Quads.
1973–1975: Executive director of the Center for Independent Living in Berkeley, which opened in 1972.
1975–1983: Director of the California Department of Rehabilitation.
1983: Co-founded the World Institute on Disability; 1984: MacArthur Fellowship; March 14, 1995: died.

people.name: Judith Heumann
body: On April 5, 1977, people with disabilities and their allies entered the federal building at 50 United Nations Plaza in San Francisco and refused to leave. They stayed for more than three weeks. One of their leaders was Judith Heumann, a teacher from Brooklyn.

The protesters wanted the government to sign rules putting Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 into effect. Section 504 said that programs receiving federal money could not discriminate against people with disabilities. For four years, the government had delayed the regulations needed to enforce it. On April 28, 1977, Secretary of Health, Education, and Welfare Joseph Califano signed them.

Heumann was born on December 18, 1947, in Philadelphia and grew up in Brooklyn, New York. She contracted polio at about 18 months old and used a wheelchair. As an adult, New York City denied her a teaching license because of her disability. At 22 she sued the city's teaching board and won, becoming the city's first teacher who used a wheelchair.
Section 504 was an early step toward the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990, which requires accessibility in workplaces, transportation and public places across the country.

Heumann later co-founded the World Institute on Disability with Ed Roberts and Joan Leon. She served as Assistant Secretary for Special Education and Rehabilitative Services in the U.S. Department of Education under President Bill Clinton, and from 2010 to 2017 as Special Advisor for International Disability Rights at the State Department under President Barack Obama. She died in Washington, D.C., on March 4, 2023.
keyFacts: December 18, 1947: Born in Philadelphia; grew up in Brooklyn, New York.
Around 1970: Won a lawsuit to become New York City's first teacher who used a wheelchair.
April 5, 1977: The Section 504 sit-in she helped lead began in San Francisco.
April 28, 1977: Section 504 regulations signed.
1993–2001: Assistant Secretary of Education for Special Education and Rehabilitative Services.
March 4, 2023: Died.

people.name: Sonia Sotomayor
body: When Sonia Sotomayor was about seven years old, living in the Bronx, New York, doctors told her family she had type 1 diabetes. She learned to give herself insulin injections as a child.

Sotomayor was born on June 25, 1954, in the South Bronx to parents from Puerto Rico. Puerto Rico is a U.S. territory, and people born there are U.S. citizens. Her father died when she was nine. Her mother, Celina, a nurse, raised Sonia and her brother, first in the Bronxdale Houses public housing project.

Sotomayor attended Princeton University on a full scholarship, graduating summa cum laude in 1976, and earned her law degree from Yale Law School in 1979. She worked as an assistant district attorney in Manhattan from 1979 to 1984 and then in private practice. In 1992 she became a federal trial judge, and in 1998 she joined the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit.

The U.S. Supreme Court is the country's highest court. Its nine justices serve for life and decide cases about the meaning of the Constitution, including civil rights, disability rights and government services.

President Barack Obama nominated Sotomayor to the Supreme Court in 2009. The Senate confirmed her by a vote of 68 to 31, and she took office on August 8, 2009, the first Hispanic justice and the third woman on the Court. As of October 2026 she is an associate justice. She has written books for adults and children, including her 2013 memoir, My Beloved World.
keyFacts: June 25, 1954: Born in the South Bronx, New York, to Puerto Rican parents.
About age 7: Diagnosed with type 1 diabetes; her father died when she was 9.
1976: Graduated from Princeton University; 1979: earned a law degree from Yale.
1992: Appointed a federal district judge; 1998: joined the Second Circuit Court of Appeals.
August 8, 2009: Took office as the first Hispanic Supreme Court justice, after a 68–31 vote.

people.name: Rachel Carson
body: In 1936, a young marine biologist named Rachel Carson took a job at the U.S. Bureau of Fisheries. She was only the second woman the bureau had hired. Her assignment sounds modest: writing radio scripts and public materials about ocean life. It joined the two things she was best at, science and writing.

Carson was born on May 27, 1907, on a farm in Springdale, Pennsylvania. She graduated magna cum laude from the Pennsylvania College for Women (now Chatham University) in 1929, studied at the marine laboratory in Woods Hole, Massachusetts, and earned a master's degree in zoology from Johns Hopkins University in 1932.

She stayed with the federal fisheries service for 15 years and rose to become editor-in-chief of all publications for the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service. In her own time she wrote books about the sea for general readers: Under the Sea Wind (1941), The Sea Around Us (1951) and The Edge of the Sea (1955).

Her most famous book, Silent Spring, appeared in 1962. It warned that chemical pesticides sprayed widely after World War II were harming birds, wildlife and possibly people. In the 1950s the U.S. had few national environmental laws. Carson's book started a national public debate about whether industry and government were protecting the public.

Carson died on April 14, 1964, at her home in Silver Spring, Maryland, less than two years after Silent Spring was published. In 1980 she was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom after her death.
keyFacts: May 27, 1907: Born in Springdale, Pennsylvania.
1932: Earned a master's in zoology from Johns Hopkins University.
1936: Hired by the U.S. Bureau of Fisheries, its second woman hire; later editor-in-chief at the Fish and Wildlife Service.
1941, 1951, 1955: Published Under the Sea Wind, The Sea Around Us and The Edge of the Sea.
1962: Silent Spring published; April 14, 1964: died at home in Silver Spring, Maryland.
1980: Presidential Medal of Freedom, after her death.

people.name: Grace Murray Hopper
body: In December 1943, in the middle of World War II, a Yale-trained mathematics professor named Grace Hopper joined the U.S. Navy's Women's Reserve. The Navy sent her to Harvard, where she worked under Howard Aiken programming the Mark I, one of the earliest large computers. She wrote its user manual, which ran to 561 pages.

Hopper was born in New York City on December 9, 1906. She earned a bachelor's degree in mathematics and physics from Vassar College in 1928, then a master's (1930) and a Ph.D. in mathematics (1934) from Yale.

Her greatest idea was that computers should understand something closer to human language, not only strings of numbers. By 1952 her team had developed A-0, a compiler, a program that translates human-written instructions into machine code. She later championed COBOL, a business programming language introduced in 1959, which went on to run business and government systems for decades.

Her career shows the close ties between the American military, universities and private industry in building computing, and that women were central to early computing when few held technical leadership jobs.
Hopper retired from the Navy as a rear admiral in 1986, at age 79. She died on January 1, 1992. In 2016 she was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom after her death.

1928: B.A., Vassar; 1930 and 1934: M.A. and Ph.D. in mathematics, Yale.
December 1943: Joined the Navy's Women's Reserve; programmed the Harvard Mark I.
1952: Her team developed the A-0 compiler.
1959: COBOL introduced; she promoted its adoption.
1986: Retired a rear admiral at 79; January 1, 1992: died; 2016: Presidential Medal of Freedom.

people.name: George C. Marshall
people.field: Military leadership, diplomacy and international affairs
body: On June 5, 1947, U.S. Secretary of State George C. Marshall spoke to the graduating class at Harvard University. Europe was still in ruins two years after World War II. In his speech Marshall proposed that the United States help rebuild it. That idea became the Marshall Plan.

Marshall was born in Uniontown, Pennsylvania, in 1880. He graduated from the Virginia Military Institute in 1901 and was commissioned a second lieutenant in the U.S. Army. President Franklin D. Roosevelt chose him as Army Chief of Staff, and he led the Army through World War II, reaching five-star rank in 1944.

After the war, he led a mediation mission to China in late 1945. President Truman then made him Secretary of State; he took office on January 21, 1947. Congress passed the Economic Cooperation Act in March 1948 to fund the Marshall Plan, and aid eventually rose to more than $12 billion for rebuilding Western Europe.
The plan rested on an argument of its time: that U.S. security depended on the economic recovery and stability of its allies, not only on military strength.

Marshall left the State Department on January 20, 1949. He then served as president of the American Red Cross and, from 1950 to 1951, as Secretary of Defense. In 1953 he received the Nobel Peace Prize. He died on October 16, 1959, at Walter Reed General Hospital in Washington, D.C.

1901: Graduated from the Virginia Military Institute; commissioned in the Army.
World War II: Army Chief of Staff under Roosevelt; five-star general in 1944.
January 21, 1947 – January 20, 1949: Secretary of State.
June 5, 1947: Proposed European recovery aid at Harvard; Congress passed the Economic Cooperation Act in March 1948.
1950–1951: Secretary of Defense; 1953: Nobel Peace Prize; October 16, 1959: died.

people.name: Fred Rogers
body: In 1969, a soft-spoken television host from Pittsburgh testified before Congress and asked lawmakers to support better television for children. The Fred Rogers Institute says that testimony led to a sharp increase in federal funding for public television. The man was Fred Rogers, and his program, Mister Rogers' Neighborhood, had become a national public television series the year before.

Rogers was born on March 20, 1928, in Latrobe, Pennsylvania. He graduated magna cum laude from Rollins College in 1951 with a degree in music composition. He went to work in television and later joined WQED, a public television station in Pittsburgh. While working there, he studied at Pittsburgh Theological Seminary and earned a divinity degree in 1962. He was ordained a Presbyterian minister in 1963, with a charge to serve children and families through television.

Mister Rogers' Neighborhood was produced at WQED and first shown regionally. It became a national program in 1968 and ran until 2001. Each episode spoke directly and calmly to young children about feelings, friendship, fear and everyday life.

American public television is separate from commercial networks and has been supported by viewers, foundations and, historically, federal money. See the Corporation for Public Broadcasting on this page for what happened to that federal money in 2025 and 2026.

On July 9, 2002, President George W. Bush presented Rogers with the Presidential Medal of Freedom. Rogers died at his home in Pittsburgh on February 27, 2003. The Fred Rogers Institute keeps an archive of more than 22,000 items from his life and work.
keyFacts: March 20, 1928: Born in Latrobe, Pennsylvania.
1951: Graduated from Rollins College in music composition.

people.name: Edward R. Murrow
body: On March 9, 1954, CBS viewers watched a television program called See It Now. Its host, Edward R. Murrow, turned his attention to Senator Joseph McCarthy, who had been accusing many Americans of communist ties, often with little evidence. Questioning a powerful senator on national television was a risky choice.

Murrow was born on April 25, 1908, on Polecat Creek near Greensboro, in Guilford County, North Carolina. In 1937 CBS sent him to Europe to build a network of correspondents. During World War II his radio reports from London opened with the words "This . . . is London."

After the war, Murrow moved to television. With producer Fred Friendly he hosted See It Now, a weekly news program. In 1953 an episode about Milo Radulovich, an Air Force reservist, led to Radulovich being reinstated. After the conflict over the McCarthy broadcast, CBS discontinued the show.
The U.S. Constitution protects freedom of the press, and most American news outlets are privately owned rather than run by the government.

In 1961 President John F. Kennedy appointed Murrow to head the United States Information Agency, which explained American policy and culture to audiences abroad. He died on April 27, 1965, at his farm in Pawling, New York.
keyFacts: April 25, 1908: Born on Polecat Creek, Guilford County, North Carolina.
1937: Sent by CBS to Europe to build a team of correspondents.
World War II: Radio reports from London.
1953: See It Now episode led to Milo Radulovich's reinstatement.
March 9, 1954: See It Now broadcast about Senator Joseph McCarthy.
1961: Appointed head of USIA by Kennedy; April 27, 1965: died at his farm in Pawling, New York.

people.name: Justin Dart Jr.
body: On July 26, 1990, President George H. W. Bush signed the Americans with Disabilities Act. On stage with him was a man in a Stetson hat and cowboy boots, known to many as the "father" of the ADA.

Justin Whitlock Dart Jr. was born in Chicago on August 29, 1930, into a wealthy family, and contracted polio in 1948, after which he used a wheelchair. He ran businesses in Mexico and Japan, including Tupperware's Japan business, where he hired women and people with disabilities. According to the Center for Disability Rights, he and his wife, Yoshiko, resigned after U.S. executives told him to stop promoting women and end his disability advocacy.

He turned full time to disability rights. In 1981 President Ronald Reagan named him vice-chair of the National Council on Disability. He and Yoshiko toured every state, at their own expense, collecting accounts of discrimination. Those stories informed the legislation that became the ADA.
In 1998 he received the Presidential Medal of Freedom. He died at his home in Washington, D.C., in June 2002, after years of complications from post-polio syndrome and congestive heart failure.
keyFacts: August 29, 1930: Born in Chicago.
1948: Contracted polio; later had post-polio syndrome.
1981: Vice-chair of the National Council on Disability.
July 26, 1990: On stage at the ADA signing.
1998: Presidential Medal of Freedom.
June 2002: Died in Washington, D.C., at 71.
people.connectToWork: The rights you explain at work expect a person to name a disability and ask. What would that same process feel like to someone who has good reasons not to?

people.name: Lois Curtis
body: Lois Curtis had developmental disabilities and schizophrenia, and she lived in institutions and hospitals for many years. As a young woman she kept calling an attorney at Atlanta Legal Aid to have her voice heard. With Elaine Wilson, she became one of two plaintiffs in a case against the State of Georgia that reached the U.S. Supreme Court. On June 22, 1999, in Olmstead v. L.C., the Court held that unjustified segregation of people with disabilities is discrimination under the ADA.

Curtis later lived in the community, in Clarkston, Georgia, and worked as a self-employed artist. On June 20, 2011, she met President Barack Obama in the Oval Office and gave him one of her pastel self-portraits, "Girl in Orange Dress." She died of pancreatic cancer on November 3, 2022, at 55.
keyFacts: Plaintiff, with Elaine Wilson, in Olmstead v. L.C. (decided June 22, 1999).
June 20, 2011: Met President Obama and gave him a pastel self-portrait.
Self-employed artist in Clarkston, Georgia.

institutions.name: Library of Congress
body: In 1800, an act of Congress set aside money to buy books for Congress. That was the start of the Library of Congress. Fourteen years later, during the War of 1812, British troops burned the Capitol, and the small library inside was destroyed. To rebuild it, Congress bought Thomas Jefferson's personal library of 6,487 books.

The library first served lawmakers. In 1870, U.S. copyright registration and deposit were centralized at the Library, so copies of American books and other works began flowing into its collections. In 1914 it created the Legislative Reference Service to support Congress's work. Its book collection grew from 10 million to 17 million volumes between 1954 and 1975.
keyFacts: 1800: Founded with funds set aside by Congress.
1814: Burned by British forces.
1815: Congress bought Jefferson's 6,487 books.
1870: Copyright registration and deposit centralized at the Library.
1914: Legislative Reference Service created.
institutions.connectToWork: Whose records and knowledge does your agency treat as the official version? What would be missing if a person's own account were not in the file?

institutions.name: Smithsonian Institution
institutions.type: National museum, education and research complex
body: James Smithson was a British chemist and mineralogist who never visited the United States. When he died on June 27, 1829, he left his fortune to the country. On August 10, 1846, President James K. Polk signed an act of Congress establishing the Smithsonian Institution "for the increase and diffusion of knowledge among men." Its first Secretary, Joseph Henry, saw it as a center for original research in fields like physics, meteorology and natural science.

By the U.S. Census Bureau's 2026 account, the Smithsonian has about 21 museums, 21 libraries, 14 education and research centers and a zoo. It holds roughly 157 million objects, fewer than 1 percent of which are on display at any time. More than 30 million people visit each year.
keyFacts: June 27, 1829: James Smithson died, leaving his fortune to the U.S.
August 10, 1846: Act signed by President Polk established the Institution.
First Secretary: Joseph Henry.
Today: about 21 museums, 14 education and research centers and a zoo; about 157 million objects.
institutions.connectToWork: Fewer than 1 percent of the Smithsonian's objects are on display. In the story your agency tells about itself, what stays in storage, and who decides?

institutions.name: Corporation for Public Broadcasting
institutions.type: Federally created nonprofit funder of public media, now dissolved
body: Congress created the Corporation for Public Broadcasting (CPB) under the Public Broadcasting Act of 1967. Its job was to channel the federal government's investment in public broadcasting, which supported public television and radio across the country.

In the summer of 2025, President Trump and Republican lawmakers rescinded federal public media funding, clawing back more than $500 million of CPB's annual funding. CPB announced that it would shut down; most staff positions ended at the end of September, with a small team staying through January 2026 to wind down. On January 5, 2026, its board voted to dissolve the organization after 58 years, after distributing its remaining funds.
keyFacts: 1967: Created by the Public Broadcasting Act.
Summer 2025: More than $500 million of CPB's annual funding rescinded.
End of September 2025: Most staff positions ended.
January 5, 2026: Board voted to dissolve CPB after 58 years.
institutions.connectToWork: If your outreach relies on public radio or a local station to reach people, have you checked whether that station still reaches them the way it did?

institutions.name: National Council on Independent Living
body: NCIL was founded in 1982 to advance the disability-led Independent Living Movement. It represents Centers for Independent Living and Statewide Independent Living Councils, and helps them build capacity to protect the human and civil rights of people with disabilities. Its stated philosophy is that people with disabilities are the best experts on their own needs.
keyFacts: Founded 1982.
Membership organization for Centers for Independent Living and Statewide Independent Living Councils.

institutions.name: Institute on Community Integration, University of Minnesota
institutions.type: University research and training center on developmental disabilities
body: The Institute on Community Integration (ICI) was founded in 1985 and is based at the University of Minnesota in Minneapolis. Its program areas are early childhood; educational policy and practice; community living and employment; and global disability rights and inclusion. Its 11-panel exhibit in the lobby, Road to Belonging, traces the disability movement "from isolation, segregation, and institutionalization toward inclusion."

Located at the University of Minnesota, Minneapolis.
Designated a University Center on Excellence in Developmental Disability.

disability.intro: This is background for preparing questions. It does not describe any person or family. Here, American means the mainstream U.S. ideas about disability built into the laws, programs and professional training that staff work inside. It is here so you can see that frame as one frame, not a neutral default. Mainstream American is not one community: views differ by generation, region, race, faith, class and disability experience, and many Americans, including many disabled Americans, do not share these ideas. We did not find a Minnesota study of what residents believe about disability, or a national survey on it to use here. Most of the research below is conceptual rehabilitation writing that describes U.S. values by contrast with other cultures. It tells you more about how systems are built than about any person.
questions: What would a good life look like for you? Would you like your family to be part of that picture?
Who do you want involved in decisions, if anyone, and how do you want those decisions made?
What words do you use for yourself: person with a disability, disabled person, something else, or none?
Has anyone given you a diagnosis or a label? Who gave it to you, and has it helped?
What do you want a label or assessment to open up for you, and is there anything you want it to avoid?
How comfortable are you telling people here about a disability or asking for an accommodation? What would make that easier?
When a form says self-advocacy, self-direction or independent living, what do you take that to mean? Would it help if I explained what it means in practice here?
Are there people or groups you rely on, such as family, friends, a faith community or peers, that you want included in planning?

context.heading: Two explanations, both at work in your job
body: The Disability Rights Education and Defense Fund's history of the ADA says that before 1973, problems such as unemployment and lack of education were assumed to be "inevitable consequences" of the disability itself. It says Congress later recognized those problems as a result of societal barriers and prejudices.

Disability studies names these two views. The University of California, San Francisco's Office of Developmental Primary Care describes the medical model as treating disability as a defect within the individual, with professionals holding the main power to correct it. It describes the social model as locating the problem in social and physical barriers, and calling for society to change. Ask yourself which view a given rule assumes: eligibility often runs on diagnosis and functional limitation, while rights and inclusion work runs on barriers and access.

sources.label: Disability Rights Education and Defense Fund, "The History of the Americans with Disabilities Act"
UCSF Office of Developmental Primary Care, "Medical and Social Models of Disability"

context.heading: A rights frame expects people to speak up
body: The U.S. Department of Justice describes the ADA as a federal civil rights law. It covers a person with an impairment that substantially limits a major life activity, a person with a history or record of one, and a person perceived as having one. Title V bars retaliation against someone who has asserted their rights.

This frame was hard won, by people such as Judith Heumann and Justin Dart Jr. on this page. It also assumes a person is comfortable naming a disability, requesting something and confronting an institution. Explain rights and accommodations in plain language, and do not read silence as having no need.

sources.label: U.S. Department of Justice, "Introduction to the Americans with Disabilities Act"

context.heading: Independence, and who decides
body: Patricia Welch Saleeby, writing in the Review of Disability Studies, says U.S. ideas of self-determination generally involve individualism, competition, future orientation and self-help, and calls independent living and least restrictive environment commonly used U.S. strategies. She reports professionals setting goals that did not fit individual and family beliefs, and families then keeping issues private, and she suggests family goal setting as one alternative. David Leake and James Skouge, in the same journal, report that 26 federally funded U.S. self-determination projects named personal attributes "congruent with American individualism" as essential. Neither article shows a year on the page, and both are conceptual, not surveys.

The independent living movement offers a different reading from inside the same culture. The National Council on Independent Living describes disabled people as the best experts on their own needs. Peer-run Centers for Independent Living grew out of that idea. So before you write independence as a goal, ask what it means to this person. Living alone or deciding alone may not be the goal, and deciding with family can be a person's own choice.

sources.label: Saleeby, "The Need for Culturally Appropriate Strategies in Promoting Self-Determination Among Individuals with Disabilities," Review of Disability Studies
Leake and Skouge, "'Self-Determination' as a Social Construct: Cross-cultural Considerations," Review of Disability Studies
National Council on Independent Living, About

context.heading: Words that may not travel
body: U.S. law and agencies mostly use person-first language, such as people with disabilities. Some disabled people prefer identity-first language, such as disabled person. Follow each person's own choice.

Leake and Skouge list terms such as self-advocacy, self-direction and self-reliance among the attributes of self-determination, and note that these terms are rarely associated with collectivistic values. When you work through an interpreter, check that independent living, least restrictive and similar terms have been explained and not just translated word for word.

sources.label: Leake and Skouge, "'Self-Determination' as a Social Construct: Cross-cultural Considerations," Review of Disability Studies
U.S. Department of Justice, "Introduction to the Americans with Disabilities Act"

context.heading: Institutions, Olmstead and Minnesota's plan
body: U.S. systems also carried out stigma through institutions. Lois Curtis, on this page, lived in institutions and hospitals for many years before Olmstead v. L.C. (1999), in which the Supreme Court held that unjustified segregation of disabled people is discrimination under the ADA.

Minnesota's Olmstead Plan takes its name from that ruling, but by the Arc Minnesota's account it came from a different case: the state agreed to create it in settling Jensen v. Minnesota Department of Human Services. The federal court approved the plan on September 29, 2015, and the Arc describes it as applying to all Minnesota government agencies. A further update was in draft in 2026.

sources.label: Legal Information Institute, Cornell, Olmstead v. L.C., syllabus
U.S. District Court, District of Minnesota, "Olmstead Plan"
The Arc Minnesota, "The Arc Guide to Olmstead Plan"

context.heading: What to check in your own forms and plans
body: These are questions for you and your team, not findings. Which words in your forms assume a person decides alone? Do your plans count a faith community, extended family or peer network as a real support, or as informal and secondary? Which goal would you write without thinking, and where did you learn that it was the right one?

organizations.intro: These are starting points for learning about civic, service and veterans groups and news outlets that are easy to take for granted as simply how things work. Asking who started them, who belongs and who they reach is one way to see a norm as a norm. The list is not complete. It does not cover Greater Minnesota TV stations, and most founding years are not given because they could not be confirmed. Listing here says nothing about who a person trusts.

entries.purpose: Describes itself as more than 120 trained and certified county veterans service officers, who offer advocacy, counseling and claims help. They are a local entry point for veterans' benefits.

entries.purpose: Service officers help veterans file VA claims and appeals for free. The department runs local chapters and auxiliary units across the state.
